title: Cue-Taking in Congress: Interest Group Signals from Dear Colleague Letters
venue: American Journal of Political Science, 63(1), pp. 163-180 (online 2018)

research_question: Why do some bills move forward while others languish? Do interest group endorsements listed in Dear Colleague letters signal bill quality to members of Congress, and does their effect vary across the legislative process?
theory: Cue-taking under limited information: members with limited time and staff rely on informative signals, and interest group endorsements are cheap, quick cues. H1 and H1a: endorsements from well-connected groups (high eigenvector centrality) are informative, most strongly early in the process. H2 and H2a: the number of endorsing groups matters more later, because it signals broad support and a larger lobbying ground game. Builds on Hall and Deardorff (2006) on lobbying as legislative subsidy and on the Kingdon cue literature.
data: Electronic Dear Colleague letters sent between House members, 106th to 111th Congresses (1999-2010): 93,967 letters, of which 6,633 bills had letters urging support. Unit is the bill. 27 percent of bills with letters had letters naming interest groups. Endorsing organizations matched to 11,019 organizations in the Amicus Curiae Networks Project plus hand-added names. Outcomes (cosponsors, reported from House committee, passed House) and sponsor data from the Congressional Bills Project. Hot Bills list from the Senate Library. Regression N = 6,597.
method: Negative binomial regression of the cosponsor count with Congress fixed effects (Table 3; AIC 60,835.04). Logit models for Reported House and Passed House (Table 4), each including cosponsor count as a regressor to capture an indirect path from social power to passage. Standard errors in parentheses; significance stars.
identification: No causal identification design (no instrument, natural experiment, or bill-level panel). Associational estimates with Congress fixed effects, sponsor and bill controls, and the cosponsor count entered as a downstream regressor. Footnote 11 notes that solicited and group-initiated endorsements cannot be distinguished.
scope: US House of Representatives only; bills that were the subject of Dear Colleague letters urging support, 1999-2010 (106th to 111th Congresses). Not the full population of introduced bills, and not the Senate, except that robustness on all bills in the 111th Congress is reported in supporting information (not in the text file).

key_findings.finding: Early stage: bills endorsed by well-connected groups attract more cosponsors. Interest Group Social Power has a positive, significant effect on the cosponsor count.
key_findings.numbers: coef 0.055 (SE 0.011), p<.001; predicted cosponsors 33 with unconnected endorsers, 38 with an endorser at centrality 2.51 (Anti-Defamation League), 51 with one at 7.66 (Planned Parenthood)

key_findings.finding: Breadth also raises early cosponsorship: each additional endorsing group adds cosponsors. Matching one moderately connected endorser takes 19 low-centrality groups.
key_findings.numbers: Interest Group Count coef 0.007 (SE 0.001), p<.001; 61 average-centrality endorsers match the 51 predicted for a Planned Parenthood-level endorsement

key_findings.finding: Social power has no significant direct effect on committee reporting or floor passage. The authors describe a single well-connected endorsement as no longer enough late in the process.
key_findings.numbers: Reported House 0.020 (SE 0.031); Passed House -0.035 (SE 0.032); both not significant

key_findings.finding: Breadth matters at the floor stage: the number of endorsing groups significantly predicts House passage but not committee reporting.
key_findings.numbers: Passed House 0.013 (SE 0.004), p<.001; Reported House 0.004 (SE 0.003), not significant

key_findings.finding: Predicted passage probability rises with the number of endorsing groups, though slowly.
key_findings.numbers: predicted probability 0.09 with no endorsements, 0.10 with 10 groups, 0.20 with 75 groups

key_findings.finding: Cosponsorship is an indirect channel from social power to success: cosponsor count predicts both committee reporting and passage.
key_findings.numbers: cosponsors coef 0.002 (SE 0.001), p<.01 for Reported House; 0.004 (SE 0.001), p<.001 for Passed House

key_findings.finding: Hot bills and commemorative bills attract more cosponsors; hot bills and majority-party sponsors are more likely to pass.
key_findings.numbers: hot bill cosponsors coef 0.365 (p<.001), about 15 additional cosponsors; commemorative bills average 78 cosponsors vs 33; Passed House: hot bill 2.428, majority 1.353, both p<.001

key_findings.finding: Network measure example: standardized eigenvector centrality in the amicus curiae network separates well-connected groups from peripheral ones.
key_findings.numbers: NOW 8.2962; NEA 2.6653; AFL-CIO 0.8824; AHA -0.1095; ASA -0.2053 (set as the minimum for groups absent from the network)

key_findings.finding: Sample scale: Dear Colleague letter volume rose sharply over the period.
key_findings.numbers: 31,994 electronic letters in the 111th Congress vs 15,477 in the 109th (up 106.7 percent)

key_findings.finding: Hypothesis pattern: H1a (social power stronger early) and H2a (breadth stronger late) are both supported as stated by the authors.
key_findings.numbers: early social power significant, late social power not; early count significant, late count significant for passage only

key_findings.finding: Conclusion on pluralism: well-connected groups act as early gatekeepers, but broad multi-group support is necessary for passage.

limitations: Endorsements may be solicited by a member's office or initiated by the group; letters do not reveal which (footnote 11, p. 171).

Endorser names were matched to the amicus network and hand-checked; groups absent from the network receive the minimum centrality score, which the authors say understates their influence (footnote 18, p. 173).
The amicus curiae network is used as a proxy for legislative relationships; the authors assume judicial and legislative relationships persist across branches (footnote 15, p. 172).

The analysis is restricted to bills that were the subject of Dear Colleague letters, with opposition letters removed (footnote 14, p. 171). Results for all bills appear only in supporting information.
Hot bill status may be determined after endorsements, which complicates its use as a control (footnote 21, p. 175).
Some letters are purpose-coded from a hand-coded subsample of 4,656 letters (footnote 9, p. 169).
Endorsing groups may not interact with one another, so endorsement lists do not establish coordination (p. 172).
The authors report no systematic per-Congress pattern in the social power and count effects (footnote 22, p. 175).
Associational results; no causal design. The authors describe the results as complex and open new questions (p. 178).
measures: Cosponsors: count of cosponsors in the Congress
Reported House and Passed House: binary outcomes from the Congressional Bills Project
Interest Group Social Power: maximum standardized eigenvector centrality among endorsing groups (amicus curiae network)
Interest Group Count: number of endorsing groups named in the letter
Hot Bills: Senate Library Hot Bills List
Majority, Seniority, Referring Committee, Committee Chair, Ranking Member: sponsor characteristics
Ideological Extremity: absolute difference between first-dimension DW-NOMINATE score and chamber median

paul_markup.text: Why do some pieces of legislation move forward while others languish?

We demonstrate that endorsements from particularly well-connected interest groups are a strong cue for members with limited information early in the legislative process and help grow the list of bill cosponsors.
However, the challenges of doing so with imperfect information have been well documented
Even if they read every bill, members cannot be expected to effectively comprehend the implications of complicated legislative text across a broad array of policy issues.
we identify the interest groups who have endorsed legislation and determine the impact of those endorsements at multiple stages of the legislative process.
By contrast, endorsements from a larger number of groups are better indicators of success later in the process when members need to amass a winning coalition of 218 votes.
devote more of their limited time to fundraising, and have fewer policy staff to support them.
Nowhere in this allocation is time for reviewing legislation introduced by other members or any sort of policy analysis.
As a result, there has been a steady decline in the number of issues Congress can address and its capacity for gathering the information necessary to create policy
Members also rely on interest groups to provide the information they need to make policy decisions.
This information is invaluable to members making voting decisions.
Therefore, a member who is concerned with the approval of a particular interest group will know that a bill is safe to support if it has their endorsement.
Some organizations are more influential than others because they have more resources, greater name recognition, or better connections within the interest group community.
The strength of their relationships with other organizations means they are likely to be well known and in a position to influence other groups.
Members of Congress work to gain the support of stakeholders when they introduce a bill because they expect it will increase the likelihood of success.
Put simply, we expect that when a bill is endorsed by a large number of organizations, the endorsements collectively demonstrate broad support for the policy in question
In addition to signaling that a bill has broad support, endorsements from a large number of organizations translate into a larger ground game.
In what follows, we test whether interest group endorsements play a role in the decision to cosponsor legislation and a bill's success in the House of Representatives.
It can be a crucial factor in building support for legislation, as it is a great way to disseminate what outside organizations are supporting legislation
Fourteen percent of the Dear Colleague letters are from members asking their colleagues to sign a letter to the administration, committee chairs, or congressional leadership.

Members of Congress and their staff have to reach out to organizations they think may be interested in supporting the bill, provide them with the legislative language prior to introduction, wait for the organization to review the bill
If nearly every bill introduced was endorsed by an interest group, the value of those signals would be significantly weakened,
In contrast, the interest groups that have endorsed a bill and are listed together on a Dear Colleague letter may not have any interaction.
As reported by the interest groups themselves, the relationships demonstrated by the cosigning of an amicus curiae brief before the Court do not disappear when those groups are lobbying Congress.
Interest groups with strong connections to other prominent and well-connected organizations have a great deal of social power within the interest group community.
NOW has more social power than the other three organizations, and therefore an endorsement from them is going to send a stronger signal to the average member of Congress than one from the ASA
Interest Group Social Power, which is the largest standardized eigenvector centrality score of the interest groups that have endorsed a bill.
That is, maximum eigenvector centrality allows us to examine whether members are swayed by a single endorsement from a powerful interest group
We expect legislation designated as a hot bill is more likely to pass the House and be signed into law.
The average bill with no endorsements is estimated to have 33 cosponsors.

It takes 61 endorsements from interest groups with no more than the average eigenvector centrality score to match the 51 cosponsors predicted for a bill endorsed by one of the groups with the greatest social power
securing an endorsement from a single socially powerful organization is the best strategy to build support for his or her legislation
As expected, Interest Group Count is positive and statistically significant in predicting whether a bill passes the House
Members have fewer bills competing for their attention, they are receiving input from more sources as multiple interest groups engage in direct lobbying, and the stakes are higher
In the earliest stages of the legislative process, bills that are vetted by an outside organization of high social power send a strong signal that they are worth considering
do not appear to have a direct effect at the end of the legislative process
Indeed, it takes a relatively large list of groups to have a substantively meaningful effect on the probability of passage.
Legislators in search of cosponsors would be wise to find a particularly well-connected group to note in their Dear Colleague letters.

the organizations that build stronger connections and are better positioned within the interest group community are more influential, particularly when legislators' time and information are the most scarce.
However, broad support from multiple interests is necessary for bill passage, suggesting that pluralism, or at least the appearance of it, is alive and well in the end.
